/-!
# Erdős Problem 275

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/275](https://www.erdosproblems.com/275)
- [CrVE70] R.B. Crittenden and C.L. Vanden Eynden, *Any n arithmetic progressions covering the first
  2^n integers cover all integers*, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 24 (1970), 475-481.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Set

namespace Erdos275

/--
If a finite system of $r$ congruences $\{ a_i\pmod{n_i} : 1\leq i\leq r\}$ (the $n_i$ are not
necessarily distinct) covers $2^r$ consecutive integers then it covers all integers.

This is best possible as the system $2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$ shows. This was proved independently by
Selfridge and Crittenden and Vanden Eynden [CrVE70].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos275.lean"]
theorem erdos_275 (r : ℕ) (a : Fin r → ℤ) (n : Fin r → ℕ)
    (H : ∃ k : ℤ, ∀ x ∈ Ico k (k + 2 ^ r), ∃ i, x ≡ a i [ZMOD n i]) (x : ℤ) :
    ∃ i, x ≡ a i [ZMOD n i] := by
  sorry

end Erdos275

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement permits zero moduli, for which Int.ModEq is equality and the congruence class is a singleton, rather than restricting to the conventional positive moduli.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The positive-modulus statement is an immediate restriction. Conversely, assume that statement and fix an integer x whose coverage is required. Replace each zero modulus n i by |a i - x| + 1, leaving positive moduli unchanged. Every originally covered integer remains covered, so the same interval hypothesis holds for this positive-modulus family. Its conclusion covers x. If the chosen class originally had modulus zero, the new congruence says |a i - x| + 1 divides a i - x, forcing a i = x; hence the original singleton also covers x. Thus the unrestricted and positive-modulus statements are equivalent. This equivalence was proved independently in /workspace/review/scratch.lean; its axioms exclude sorryAx.

review.notes: The sole theorem faithfully states the covering result. The quantifiers, repeated moduli, integer domain, and interval length agree with the source. Lean checks established that r = 0 cannot satisfy the hypothesis, modulus one gives legitimate covering examples, and the sharpness example covers 1 through 2^r−1 but not 2^r. Exhaustive bounded tests for r ≤ 3 also passed. The current source's PROVED (LEAN) status agrees with the metadata. The linked proof has the identical statement and no sorry or custom axioms; it was inspected, not rebuilt with its older Lean toolchain. Direct source/PDF requests were blocked, so the source page was read through a text reader and the 1970 paper's introduction through OpenAlex.
